reasons: SCHEMA MISMATCH DISABLES THE DEADLY WARNING. The entry uses `severity` on each lookalike; `ForageSpecies`/`Lookalike` in /Users/dmarzari/Server-Sites/Cookbook/src/data/foraging.ts defines the field as `danger` with enum 'deadly' | 'toxic' | 'unpalatable'. /Users/dmarzari/Server-Sites/Cookbook/src/components/ForageSection.tsx:69 computes `const deadly = s.lookalikes.filter((l) => l.danger === 'deadly')` — with `severity` that returns [], so the collapsed-row banner 'Confusable with Canada moonseed — read before picking' (line 92-94) NEVER RENDERS, the deadly border styling at line 108 is lost, and `{l.danger}` at line 110 renders blank on all six rows. The single most important safety affordance in the component is silently switched off. 'harmless' is also not a legal value (three lookalikes use it).

MONTHS ARE OFF BY ONE — THE SCHEMA IS 0-INDEXED. foraging.ts documents `/** Peak months, 0 = January. */` and `forageFor()` filters `s.months.includes(month)`. Peer entries confirm it: Ramps [2,3,4] = Mar-May, Black walnut [8,9,10] = Sep-Nov. This entry's [4,5,6,7,8,9] therefore publishes as MAY-OCTOBER. Its own harvest text says April is 'a real filé month' on the Gulf Coast and in east Texas, and that autumn leaves 'are low in mucilage and make weak filé'. As submitted the entry is invisible in April — its flagship southern month — and surfaced in October, which its own text disclaims.

CAUTION LEVEL IS WRONG BY THE PROJECT'S OWN DEFINITION. foraging.ts: `expert` = 'a deadly lookalike exists', `care` = 'has confusable neighbours that will make you ill', and CAUTION_LABEL renders `expert` as the literal string 'deadly lookalike exists'. This entry marks Canada moonseed deadly in its own lookalike list, so it is categorically `expert`. Corpus calibration agrees — stinging nettle and garlic mustard are already `expert`, while `care` is reserved for dandelion, violet and black walnut. Miscoding it also demotes it in `forageFor()`, which sorts expert-first specifically so the warnings lead.

MISSING SERIOUSLY TOXIC LOOKALIKE: MOUNTAIN LAUREL AND THE ENTIRE-LEAVED ERICACEAE. The entry's own `indicator` field sends the forager toward it — 'a floor of lowbush blueberry, huckleberry or mountain laurel marks the dry acid upland it favours' — and `habitat` lists mountain laurel as an associate. Kalmia latifolia passes EVERY discriminator the entry supplies: it is simple (the compound-vs-simple poison ivy rule misses it), entire-margined (the toothed-margin mulberry rule misses it), latex-free, self-supporting (the moonseed habit rule misses it), and non-aromatic. All parts carry grayanotoxins, which are heat-stable and survive drying and grinding — i.e. survive filé processing — causing vomiting, bradycardia, hypotension, and in severe cases coma or death. Rhododendron maximum, sheep laurel, Lyonia and Leucothoe share the same trap. For an entry whose entire safety architecture is 'sort every leaf individually before drying', omitting the one dangerous plant that passes all the sorting rules is disqualifying.

MISSING LOOKALIKE: BLACK CHERRY (Prunus serotina), named twice in the entry's own habitat text as a co-occurring associate in old-field succession and dune-back thickets. It suckers at exactly picking height with simple, alternate, elliptic leaves, and its cyanogenic glycosides release HCN on WILTING AND DRYING — precisely the entry's preparation step. It is caught only by the toothed-margin test, which the entry attaches solely to mulberry and never generalises.

CITATION MISATTRIBUTED AND OVERSTATED ON THE LOAD-BEARING CLAIM. J AOAC Int 80(5):1023 (1997), PMID 9325580, is by Carlson M. and Thompson R.D. — not 'Carlin M. et al.' The paper reports safrole '< LOD for most leaf samples' across 26 samples (root-bark teas 0.09-4.66 mg/cup, one oil at 92.4%), which does not support the entry's flat assertion of 'no detectable safrole in sassafras leaf'. The direction of the claim holds and the 21 CFR 189.180 / 172.580 reading is correct, but the sentence that licenses this entire entry must match its source.

POISON OAK GEOGRAPHIC UNDER-WARNING. The entry calls Atlantic poison oak 'specifically a southeastern and Coastal Plain problem' and the harvest text scopes it to 'the Southeast'. Toxicodendron pubescens is documented in IL, MO, KS, OK, TX, TN and WV — inside this entry's own `midwest` region and inside the range its habitat text claims (eastern Kansas, eastern Oklahoma, eastern Texas). A Missouri or southern Illinois forager is told the harder-to-spot urushiol plant is not their problem, in an entry that elsewhere calls poison oak 'the harder of the two'.

REGIONS OMIT `southcentral`. REGIONS in /Users/dmarzari/Server-Sites/Cookbook/src/data/seasonal-regional.ts maps TX and OK to `southcentral`, and `regionForState` routes those users there. The entry's range covers eastern Oklahoma and eastern Texas and its timing advice is built around 'mid-to-late March on the Gulf Coast and in east Texas' — yet no Texas or Oklahoma reader will ever be shown the entry. Either add `southcentral` or drop the east-Texas timing as the headline case.

Everything else holds up on independent check and should be preserved: `Sassafras albidum (Nutt.) Nees` is the correct, unambiguous accepted name and the sole North American Sassafras; the moonseed tells (subpeltate petiole, palmate shallow lobes, twining habit, dauricine) are accurate and it is correctly rated deadly; the simple-vs-compound urushiol rule with eyes-before-hands and no crush-test is exactly right; leaf-only scoping with the root/root-bark firewall is correct; and 'no treatment required for safety' is accurate for sassafras leaf, so no required preparation step is omitted.
